extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, formalizers, and contributors/users of the Mizar proof assistant and Mizar Mathematical Library (MML)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing formal mathematical definitions and proofs in the Mizar language so they are mechanically checked by the Mizar proof checker and (optionally) accepted into the Mizar Mathematical Library after peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability / closeness to mathematical vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctive feature of the Mizar language is its readability. Mizar articles are written in ordinary ASCII, but the language was designed to be close enough to the mathematical vernacular that most mathematicians could read and understand Mizar articles without special training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design proofs and definitions to be clear and close to standard mathematical prose; this facilitates human reading and uptake even though extra formal detail will be necessary for checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical logic and declarative style
rubrics_metrics.description: As is common in mathematical text, Mizar relies on classical logic and a declarative style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author proofs in a declarative manner consistent with classical logic conventions expected by Mizar; procedural/imperative proof styles are not the norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof admission: justify every proof step
rubrics_metrics.description: For a proof to be admitted, all steps have to be justified either by elementary logical arguments or by citing previously verified proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every inference is either given a direct logical justification or references an existing verified theorem in the MML; omissions or unjustified leaps will prevent admission by the checker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference and reuse of Mizar Mathematical Library (MML)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MML includes all theorems to which authors can refer in newly written articles. Authors refer to the MML theorems in proofs; once approved by the proof checker they may be further evaluated for inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authoring, search MML for existing theorems to cite rather than re-proving; structure new items to interoperate with and cite the MML to ease verification and integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review for contribution and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Once approved by the proof checker MML entries are further evaluated in a process of peer-review for appropriate contribution and style. If accepted they are published in the Journal of Formalized Mathematics and added to the MML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond mechanical correctness, submissions should meet community expectations for mathematical contribution and presentation style to be accepted into the canonical library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher rigor/detail and expected verbosity (de Bruijn factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: This results in a higher level of rigor and detail than is customary in mathematical textbooks and publications. Thus, a typical Mizar article is about four times as long as an equivalent paper written in ordinary style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for substantially more detail and length when formalizing; aim to expand intuitions into fully justified steps. Expect greater labor per page of informal text (the page notes ~one week full-time to verify a textbook page once versed in the system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical foundations and typing discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The MML is built on the axioms of the Tarski–Grothendieck set theory. Even though semantically all objects are sets, the language allows one to define and use syntactical weak types. For example, a set may be declared to be of type Nat only when its internal structure conforms with a particular list of requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the underlying Tarski–Grothendieck axioms and the Mizar type-declaration mechanisms when defining objects; types are syntactic devices that enforce structural requirements and reflect mathematicians' usual distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability, distribution, and contribution workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: All MML articles are available in PDF form as the papers of the Journal of Formalized Mathematics. The full text of the MML is distributed with the Mizar checker and can be freely downloaded. An experimental wiki form admits edits only when they are approved by the Mizar checker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provided PDFs and the distributed MML for reference; contributions can be developed locally with the checker and, if applicable, submitted via the project's workflow (including wiki edits that must pass the checker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software licensing and usage restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributions of the Mizar Proof Checker are freely available for major operating systems. Use of the proof checker is free for all non-commercial purposes. It is written in Free Pascal and the source code is available on GitHub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the non-commercial usage restriction for the checker; consult project/license documentation for commercial use. Obtain and build the checker from the provided distributions or GitHub source as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searchability / MML Query capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The MML Query website implements a powerful search engine for the contents of the MML. Among other abilities, it can retrieve all MML theorems proved about any particular type or operator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MML Query to locate relevant theorems, operators, and prior formalizations to inform and shorten your own formalization work and to avoid duplication.
